A lookup page, for the moment a query fails with an unknown-function error and you need to know whether the function is missing or your spelling is. Nothing here is worth reading in advance. If you are trying to decide where spatial work should run, that is [Join and transform polygons](../howdoi/polygons.qmd) instead, and it explains why the answer is usually the server.

## Ask your own compute, rather than trusting a list

```sql
SHOW FUNCTIONS LIKE 'st_*'
```

That is the whole answer, and it is the only thing on this page that cannot go stale. Run it on the compute you are actually connected to and count what comes back.

This beats any published figure, including the ones below. The platform's own documented count moved from "80+" to "90+" inside a year, so a number written down anywhere is a claim about a date rather than a fact about your compute. The names also differ between one kind of compute and another, which the next section covers, so a count from someone else's cluster is not a count from yours.

One practical note. On a cluster, run the statement through Spark rather than wrapping it in `SELECT count(*)`, which is not valid there. That one-line difference reads as "spatial support is broken" when it is nothing of the sort.

## What was there when this was measured

`r wq_fact("spatial_functions_warehouse", "words")` distinct functions on a Pro warehouse running serverless, and `r wq_fact("spatial_functions_cluster")` on an all-purpose cluster, measured on 2026-08-24.

Both numbers need the compute attached, always, because the gap between them is the point of the page.

The count also needs its definition next to it, or it means nothing: four different figures were in circulation before this was pinned down. `r wq_fact("spatial_functions_warehouse", "words")` is distinct names, with no aliases inflating it and no separate geography family counted twice, since most functions take either type in one signature. Two of the `r wq_fact("spatial_functions_warehouse")` are aggregates and five are geography constructors. Counting only what you would call a spatial operation gives the same `r wq_fact("spatial_functions_warehouse")`.

## The cluster has fewer, not more

Four functions exist on the warehouse and not on an all-purpose cluster:

- `st_makepoint()`
- `st_makeenvelope()`
- `st_pointonsurface()`
- `st_collect()`

Nothing exists on the cluster that is absent from the warehouse, so it is a strict subset.

This is the entry most likely to save you an afternoon, because the direction is backwards from what anyone assumes: the larger, more expensive compute has the smaller spatial vocabulary. Code written against a warehouse and moved to a cluster fails on exactly these four and on nothing else that was tested.

Use `st_point()` in place of `st_makepoint()`. It exists on both and takes the same two coordinates.

The older Classic warehouse type is a third case. It is documented as not supporting these functions, and that was not confirmed here by running anything, so treat it as documented rather than measured. The exclusion appears on each function's own reference page rather than in any overview, which is why it is easy to miss.

## Absent from both, and what to do instead

About twenty `sf` staples have no server-side equivalent anywhere. The ones worth naming, because you are most likely to reach for them:

`st_makevalid()`, `st_relate()`, `st_voronoi()`, `st_snap()`, `st_segmentize()`, `st_sample()`, `st_polygonize()`, `st_shortestline()`.

`st_makevalid()` is the sharpest of these, because repairing an invalid geometry is routine in `sf` and the asymmetry here is stark: the server will tell you a polygon is invalid with `st_isvalid()` and will not fix it. Your two options are to repair the geometry before loading it, or to collect it and repair it in R.

## Reading the error you get

An unknown-function error cannot tell you whether the function is missing from your compute or was never a function at all. The message is the same either way, differing only in the name it quotes, confirmed against an invented name. So check the spelling and the compute together, rather than assuming either.

A wrong argument count is the easy case, and does produce a different error, naming how many arguments the function wanted. That is the one spatial error that tells you something specific.

## Where the semantics differ from `sf`

The divergence that costs real money lives on [Join and transform polygons](../howdoi/polygons.qmd) rather than here. Read this much even if you read nothing else on this page: on longitude and latitude, `sf` and the server model the Earth differently, and the answers differ with no error and no symptom. Measurements differ by five orders of magnitude, and true-or-false tests differ on boundaries. Projecting your coordinates fixes both. Nobody arrives at a lookup page holding a problem that has no symptom, which is why it is flagged here as well as there.

What belongs here is the set of mismatches you meet while porting an expression, which are about the shape of what comes back rather than its value:

| Function | `sf` gives you | The server gives you |
|---|---|---|
| `st_contains()` | A sparse index list | One boolean per row |
| `st_distance()` | A matrix | One scalar per row |
| `st_buffer()` | `nQuadSegs`, `endCapStyle` and companions | Two arguments, and it rejects a third |

Buffer values also differ slightly, because the two approximate a circle with a different default segment count. That is an approximation difference rather than a disagreement, so do not go hunting for a bug.

Several semantics were checked and agree: self-containment, empty geometry, and the validity of a self-intersecting polygon all match `sf`.

Containment on a boundary is the case to be careful with, because it depends on the projection and on where the point sits. A point at a polygon's corner agrees. A point on the interior of an edge does not, on longitude and latitude: `st_intersects()`, `st_covers()` and `st_touches()` are TRUE on the server and FALSE in `sf`, and `st_disjoint()` the reverse. Project the coordinates and they agree. The reason is on [Join and transform polygons](../howdoi/polygons.qmd#spatial-joins-are-affected-too-and-that-is-the-one-that-will-catch-you), and it is the same reason the measurements diverge.

## What is not settled

Two things, because you would plan differently without them.

Whether the four cluster-absent functions are a fact about one runtime version or a permanent split is unknown. It was measured once.

And the semantics of the remaining functions have not been audited against `sf`. The section above covers the cases most likely to diverge, not all of them.

## Next

If your query fails for a reason that is not a missing function, [When it breaks](when-it-breaks.qmd) is organised by symptom. If the function exists and you are deciding whether to use it or bring the geometry back to R, see [Join and transform polygons](../howdoi/polygons.qmd).
